description: Run a bash command on the user's computer and get its exit code and combined stdout and stderr. The working directory carries over between calls (a cd persists); variables, aliases and functions do not. Commands run as the user with no sandbox and no approval step. By default a command runs in the foreground with empty stdin and no terminal, and the call waits for it to finish, so don't run editors, pagers or anything that prompts that way: pass flags such as --yes or --no-pager, or set tty. A command is stopped when it runs longer than timeout_ms, 120000 by default; give a larger value for slow builds or tests, or 0 for no time limit. A foreground command still running after 2 minutes is handed back to you as a numbered process with its output so far; it keeps running, and its time limit still applies. Set tty to run the command in a terminal, for REPLs, prompts, full-screen programs or other agents' terminal interfaces; in the foreground, a terminal command also returns once its screen has been still for 10 seconds, since it may be waiting for input. Set run_in_background, with or without tty, to start a server, a watcher or any long job and get its process number within a few seconds; it then has no time limit unless you give timeout_ms. For REPLs and other programs you will keep talking to, use run_in_background, or timeout_ms 0 in the foreground. Never ask the user to paste a password or other secret into the chat, where it would reach you and the session log; when a terminal command asks for one, or needs something only a person can do, such as a browser login or a program you can't drive, call process with ask_user_to_attach so they type into it directly. Check one variable by name and list processes by number and name; don't print the whole environment or processes' arguments (env, ps aux), where any secret could reach you and the session log. When a background process ends while no turn is running, you are told in a new turn, so end your turn rather than wait for a long job. A result that gives a process number means the process tool can wait for it, read or search its output, show its screen, type into it or stop it. Programs left running with & or nohup are stopped when the command that started them exits; run them with run_in_background instead. Background processes are stopped when Wisp exits; for a server or other service that must stay up after that, also set keep_running. The full output of every call is saved to a file whose path is in the result; long output is shown only as a preview, so read the parts you need with the process tool, or from that file with sed -n, grep or tail.

command.description: The bash command or script to run.

description.description: Five to ten words on what the command does, shown to the user.

keep_running.description: With run_in_background: keep the process running after Wisp exits, for a server or service that must stay up. Its output then goes to a log file named in the result.

run_in_background.description: Start the command and return within a few seconds with its process number and first output, instead of waiting for it to finish. Without tty its stdin stays open for the process tool. It is stopped when Wisp exits unless keep_running is set.

timeout_ms.description: The command's time limit in milliseconds: it is stopped once it has run this long. 0 means no limit. Defaults to 120000 in the foreground and to no limit with run_in_background. A foreground call returns after 2 minutes at most; a longer limit keeps applying to the process it hands back.

tty.description: Run the command in a terminal, so it can prompt, draw a full screen and take keys through the process tool. Combine with run_in_background to start it without waiting.

name: bash
